memo.title: First-look diligence memo: transaction data review

claims.text: Net product revenue grew only 1.9% to £9.33M in the latest 12 months, from £9.16M in the prior 12 months.
Revenue from identified customers fell 2.0%, while revenue with no customer ID grew 32.1% to £1.40M, so the headline growth rests on sales we cannot tie to any customer.
Month-3 customer retention fell 3.9 pts for Jan–Jun 2011 cohorts versus Jan–Jun 2010 cohorts, which is a warning sign for the quality of newer customers.
The data reconciles fully: every one of 1,067,371 rows is classified once, and raw revenue of £19.29M sits £361.0k above net product revenue of £18.93M.
A total of 22,523 rows worth £377.5k were delivered twice across sheets (2.0% of raw revenue) and have been counted once.
We removed 11,812 exact duplicate lines within invoices, which could be genuine repeat scans, so this needs confirming with management.
13.1% of valid sales have no customer ID, so they are in revenue but outside all customer and cohort analysis.
Active customers grew 1.3% to 4,293 and average order value grew 1.1% to £449.75, but orders per active customer fell 4.3% to 4.11x.
Identified-customer revenue fell to £7.93M from £8.09M, so existing customers ordering less often is not offset by the small rise in customer count.
In the sales bridge, a volume effect of -£1.57M was offset mainly by £2.05M from new products and a mix effect of £577.7k, with -£704.2k lost from discontinued products.
The price effect was -£115.9k, which includes changes in discount tiers, and new products made up 21.3% of gross product sales in the latest 12 months.
Customer retention is about 21.0% at month 1 and 21.1% at month 3, then 18.4% at both month 6 and month 12.

Month-12 revenue retention of 26.4% is above customer retention of 18.4%, which may mean bigger buyers are the ones who stay, though this data cannot confirm it and only 11 cohorts have reached that age.
Month-3 retention fell from 24.0% for Jan–Jun 2010 cohorts to 20.1% for Jan–Jun 2011 cohorts.
Among 4,305 new customers with at least 90 days of history, 43.8% placed a second order within 90 days, and repeat customers account for 91.0% of identified revenue in the latest 12 months.
Sales are concentrated in customers: the top 1% account for 30.7% of identified sales and the top 10% for 60.5%, though the largest single customer is only 3.3%.
Large accounts (657 customers) provide 46.4% of identified revenue and their revenue changed by -0.6%, while small accounts (3,663 customers) provide 53.6% and their revenue fell 3.3%.
The product range is broad and not dependent on hits: the top 10 products make 8.5% of sales and 833 of 3,897 products are needed to reach 80%.
The United Kingdom accounts for 84.6% of product sales.
What are the sales with no customer ID, why did they grow 32.1%, and can they be matched to accounts?
Are the 11,812 removed duplicate lines and the 22,523 rows repeated across sheets genuine system artefacts, or real transactions?
Why did orders per active customer fall 4.3% and month-3 retention fall 3.9 pts for newer cohorts?
Are the new products, worth 21.3% of sales, replacing discontinued lines worth -£704.2k, and how are discount tiers set?
Most buyers look like trade (wholesale) accounts rather than end consumers, so conclusions about consumer demand or behaviour need care.
The 951 customers already active in the first month are excluded from retention averages, and later cohorts have fewer months of history, with 11 cohorts reaching month 12.
The data shows what changed but not why, and it holds no cost, margin or channel information, so profitability and causes of the trends cannot be assessed.
Data ends part-way through December 2011, so that month is excluded from year-over-year comparisons.
